title: Graphs: breadth-first and depth-first search
summary: Model things connected to other things, then explore them level by level (shortest paths) or branch by branch (connected areas).

sections.heading: Things and connections
body: A graph is a set of nodes (places, people, pages) joined by edges (roads, friendships, links). The usual way to store one is an adjacency list: for each node, the list of its neighbours.
Grids are graphs too: each cell is a node, and its neighbours are the cells above, below, left and right.

sections.heading: Breadth-first search: nearest first
body: BFS explores in rings: first every node 1 step away, then every node 2 steps away, and so on. So the first time it reaches the goal, it has found the fewest steps.
It needs a queue (first in, first out) and a `seen` set so no node is visited twice. In JavaScript, `shift()` is fine for small graphs; for big ones keep an index into the array instead.

sections.heading: Depth-first search: follow one path to the end
body: DFS goes as deep as it can before backing up. It does not find shortest paths, but it is the simplest way to visit everything connected to a starting point.
Counting islands on a map: scan every cell. When you find unvisited land, that is a new island; "sink" it by visiting all land connected to it, so it is not counted again.

mistakes: No `seen` set: a cycle in the graph makes the search loop forever.
Marking a node as seen when you take it off the queue instead of when you add it, so it gets queued many times.
Using DFS when you need the shortest path. Use BFS.
Checking `rows[r][c]` before checking that `r` and `c` are inside the grid.
